title: One Array, No Pointers: Heap Index Arithmetic
quickIdea: A complete binary tree in level order is an array with no holes, so a heap needs no pointers. With 1-based indices the children of i are 2i and 2i+1 and the parent is floor(i/2); with 0-based indices they are 2i+1 and 2i+2 and the parent is floor((i-1)/2).
remember: 1-based, the convention GATE usually states: root at 1, left child 2i, right child 2i+1, parent floor(i/2), last node at n.
0-based, the convention of C, Java and Python arrays: root at 0, left child 2i+1, right child 2i+2, parent floor((i-1)/2).
The mapping is exact only because the shape is complete: level order fills the array without gaps, so a node's index is decided by its place in the tree and nothing else.
Node i exists iff i <= n; its left child exists iff 2i <= n (1-based), so 'is this a leaf' is a comparison, not a walk.
The two conventions differ by one in the child indices and by a shift in the parent, and mixing them is the commonest arithmetic slip in heap questions.
Storage is Theta(n) cells with no per-node link, which is exactly what lets heapsort run in place.

example.prompt: With 1-based indices and n = 12, describe nodes 3 and 10 and name the leaves. Then give the same facts for 0-based indices.
example.work: 1-based: node 3 has children 6 and 7 and parent 1; node 10 has parent 5 and no children, because 2*10 = 20 exceeds 12; the internal nodes are 1 to floor(12/2) = 6, so the leaves are 7 to 12. 0-based: the same tree is stored at indices 0 to 11, node 3 has children 7 and 8 and parent 1, and the leaves are the indices i with 2i+1 > 11, that is 6 to 11.
example.answer: 1-based: children of 3 are 6 and 7, parent 1, leaves 7 to 12 (six leaves). 0-based: children of 3 are 7 and 8, parent 1, leaves 6 to 11 (six leaves).

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.13 asks which of four index expressions cannot name a leaf of a heap with odd n > 100; GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 Q.33 asks how many indices the maximum of a 105-key min-heap can occupy. Both are answered by one fact: with 1-based indices the internal nodes are 1 to floor(n/2) and the leaves are floor(n/2)+1 to n.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.13. Let n be an odd number greater than 100. A binary min-heap with n elements is stored in an array P whose index starts from 1. Which of the following indices of P do/does NOT correspond to any leaf node of the min-heap? (1) (n+1)/2 (2) (n-1)/2 (3) (n-3)/2 (4) n
variations.why: For odd n the internal nodes are 1 to (n-1)/2 and the leaves are (n+1)/2 to n. So (n+1)/2 is the first leaf and n is the last, while (n-1)/2 is the last internal node and (n-3)/2 = (n-1)/2 - 1 is internal too. At n = 101: leaves are 51 to 101, so 51 and 101 are leaves and 50 and 49 are internal nodes with children.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: With 0-based indices and n = 12, which indices are leaves?
variations.why: A node i has a left child at 2i+1, so it is internal exactly when 2i+1 <= 11, that is i <= 5. The internal nodes are 0 to 5 and the leaves are 6 to 11. The count agrees with the 1-based answer because the shape did not change, only the labels.

trap.what: Applying the 1-based formulas to a 0-based array, or the reverse.
trap.why: The parent of index 6 is 3 when the array starts at 1 and 2 when it starts at 0. Using the wrong one silently names the wrong node, and every later comparison in the trace is then about the wrong key.
trap.counterexample: In the 0-based array [10,8,5,3,2,1], index 4 holds 2 and its parent is floor((4-1)/2) = 1, holding 8. The 1-based formula floor(4/2) = 2 would name index 2, holding 5, which is not the parent of anything at index 4.

check.question: With 1-based indices and n = 12, which indices are leaves and how many are there?
check.explanation: Internal nodes are 1 to floor(12/2) = 6, so the leaves are 7 to 12. That is n - floor(n/2) = 12 - 6 = 6 = ceil(n/2) leaves, the count the next card uses.
